name: Tai Nüa
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Yu Cuirong & Luo Meizhen 1980, Daiyu jianzhi (concise grammar of Dai, incl. Dehong/Tai Nüa); Chinese-language grammar, no online copy reachable

sources.citation: Wang, Lu, Binghao Wang & Yao Lu. 2026. Tai Nuea. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56, e21, 1-17 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100326101108. Open Access CC BY-NC-ND.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Mangshi (Dehong dialect) speaker; sections: Consonants (17), Vowels (monophthongs, a/aː length, diphthongs, triphthongs with acoustic data), Tones (nine: T33 T35 T31 T51 T55 T24 unchecked; T23 T31 T55 checked; durations), Syllable structure (CV, CVV, CVVV, CVC, CVVC), transcribed North Wind and Sun passage with phrase-boundary marks. There is no prosody/stress/intonation section and the word 'stress' does not occur.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tai Nuea language' (accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.access_detail: read online, no copy kept
sources.note: Gives 16-17 initials, 84 finals, six tones (three or four checked); no mention of stress. Used only for its reference list (Chantanaroj 2007, Luo 1998, Zhou, Fang & Meng 1981, Zhou & Luo 2001).

sources.citation: 伍贝贝 [Wu Beibei]. 2026. 德宏傣语持续体标记研究 [A study on durative aspect markers in Dehong Dai]. 现代语言学 Modern Linguistics 14(2): 239-250. doi:10.12677/ml.2026.142136 (Hans, OA).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Grammar/aspect article; no mention of 重音/轻声 or any prosody.

sources.citation: Chantanaroj, Apiradee. 2007. A sociolinguistic survey of selected Tai Nua speech varieties. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xvi+187 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ch. 2 reviews Proto-Tai tone boxes and the Tai Nua tone system (after Gedney 1976, Robinson 1994); ch. 5 lexicostatistics over 22 varieties (Mangshi, Ruili, Yingjiang, Zhefang, Gengma, Menglian area, Jinggu, Tai Mau Nam Kham, Tai Lai of Myanmar..), stripping 'presyllables and other extra syllables' before cognate comparison; tone-split diagrams per variety. No statement on word stress; 'accent' is used only for regional accent differences.

sources.citation: Luo Yongxian. 1999. A dictionary of Dehong, Southwest China. Pacific Linguistics C-145. Canberra: ANU (xl+338 pp; CC BY-SA online edition via sealang/CRCL).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Introduction §2.1 (pp. xiii-xiv) gives consonants, vowels, diphthongs and six open-syllable tones (24, 53, 11, 31, 43, 33) plus three checked tones for Mangshi Dehong; §2.2 consonant/vowel/tone alternations; §2.3 word formation and four-syllable expressions. No statement anywhere about word stress/accent (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent/prominence hits are dictionary glosses only).

sources.citation: Northern Illinois University SEAsite, 'Tai Dehong Language and Culture' web pages (Overview, Introduction, Phonology, Tones), based on Luo 1999's introduction.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Summarises Luo's phonemic inventory and classification remarks (Robinson 1999 on Proto-Na-Khamti); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Gedney, William J. 1989 [orig. 1976]. Notes on Tai Nuea. In R.J. Bickner, J. Hartmann, T.J. Hudak & P. Peyasantiwong (eds.), Selected Papers on Comparative Tai Studies, 281-372. Ann Arbor: Center for South and Southeast Asian Studies, University of Michigan. (Originally in Gething, Harris & Kullavanijaya eds., Tai Linguistics in Honor of Fang-Kuei Li, Bangkok 1976, 62-102.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Image-only scan; scanned pp. 281-292 (whole introduction + 'Phonological Inventory'). Describes six live-syllable tones, dead-syllable tones, nine vowels + a/aa length, initials and finals of the məŋ⁴ vɔ² Tai Nuea dialect (north of Sipsongpanna); notes possible tone sandhi in checked syllables 'conditioned by the tone of the following syllable'. Nothing on stress. Rest of the paper (pp. 292-372) is a wordlist.

sources.citation: Harris, Jimmy G. 1975. A comparative word list of three Tai Nüa dialects. In J.G. Harris & J.R. Chamberlain (eds.), Studies in Tai Linguistics in Honor of William J. Gedney, 202-230. Bangkok: Central Institute of English Language.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Image-only scan; scanned pp. 202-209. Pp. 202-205 give tones (5 per dialect), vowels, initial and final consonants for Chefang (tay lə), Nam Hkam Tai Mau (tay maw) and Van Poong Tong (tay nə); 'no initial consonant clusters'. No mention of stress; remainder is the word list.

sources.note: Thai-language grammar of (Chinese) Tai Nuea by a Chulalongkorn fieldworker; Chula-tradition grammars routinely include a section on การลงเสียงหนักเบา (stress in polysyllabic words), so this is the likeliest place for an explicit stress rule.

sources.citation: Zhou Yaowen 周耀文 & Luo Meizhen 罗美珍. 2001. 傣语方言研究: 语音, 词汇, 文字 [Studies of Dai dialects: phonology, lexicon, scripts]. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe.

sources.note: The fullest modern Chinese phonological description of the Dai dialects including Dehong (Mangshi) and Menggeng Tai Nüa; if any Chinese source comments on 重音/轻声 in polysyllables or prefixes (pu-, ʔu-, tsə- etc.), it is this or the jianzhi.
